```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, out.width = "100%")
root <- if (file.exists("../outputs/tables")) ".." else "."
tab <- function(n) readr::read_csv(file.path(root, "outputs/tables", paste0(n, ".csv")), show_col_types = FALSE)
fig <- function(n) knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root, "outputs/figures", paste0(n, ".png")))
show <- function(df, digits = 3) knitr::kable(df, digits = digits, format = "html",

```

# Introduction

Electricity distribution planning depends on the ability to anticipate which households will draw
heavy load. This report analyses a household electricity dataset of **45,345 household-month records**
across **16 Indian cities** and **32 providers**. It has three objectives: to describe consumption
patterns, to model the drivers of monthly consumption, and to predict whether a household-month falls
into the **peak-demand** category.

Because the dataset records monthly totals rather than interval (hourly) meter readings, peak demand
is defined at the household-month level: a record is classed as peak demand when its monthly
consumption is at least **`r thr` hours**, the 75th percentile of the distribution.

All analysis is reproducible from the scripts in the `R/` directory and follows the topics of the
course syllabus, as mapped in `docs/syllabus_mapping.md`.

# Data and Preparation

```{r audit}
show(audit)
```

The audit shows no missing values and no duplicate records. The variable `MotorPump` is constant
(zero in every record) and was removed. The recorded bill was verified to equal monthly hours
multiplied by the tariff rate to numerical precision. This identity has a modelling consequence:
tariff and bill are excluded from the predictors of consumption, since including them would leak the
target.

Three variables were engineered: `DaysInMonth` (calendar control), `Season`, and the binary
`PeakDemand` label. A stratified sample reproduces the population peak share, confirming that
sampling does not distort the class balance.

# Exploratory Analysis

```{r f1}
fig("01_consumption_distribution")
```

Monthly consumption is symmetric and approximately bell shaped, centred near 515 hours.

```{r f2}
fig("02_monthly_profile")
```

Mean consumption varies with the number of days in the month. February (28 days) has the lowest
mean and the lowest peak share, while 31-day months have the highest.

```{r f3}
fig("08_appliance_scatter")
```

```{r f4}
fig("04_correlation_matrix")
```

Television, fan, refrigerator and monitor usage each correlate positively with consumption.
The correlation between `ElectricityBill` and `MonthlyHours` is high, while the bill also
depends on the tariff.

```{r f5}
fig("05_bill_by_city")
```

Differences in mean bill between cities are driven by the tariff rate rather than by usage:
mean consumption is nearly identical across cities (see `outputs/tables/city_summary.csv`).

```{r f6}
fig("07_peak_heatmap")
```

# Unsupervised Learning

## Household segmentation

```{r kmsel}
fig("09_kmeans_selection")
```

The silhouette criterion selects **three** segments.

```{r clu}
show(clu)
```

```{r clufig}
fig("11_cluster_profile_heatmap")
```

The segments differ mainly in monitor and fan usage. The segment with the heaviest monitor use has
a peak share of `r scales::percent(clu$PeakShare[clu$Cluster == 1], 0.1)`, compared with
`r scales::percent(clu$PeakShare[clu$Cluster == 3], 0.1)` for the segment with the lowest fan and
refrigerator levels.

## Association rules

```{r rules}
fig("12_association_rules")
```

Combinations of high fan, television and monitor usage have a lift above 2 for peak demand,
meaning such households are more than twice as likely to be peak consumers as the average household.

# Regression Models for Consumption

```{r reg}
show(reg)
```

```{r regfig}
fig("15_regression_comparison")
```

The linear model and the generalized additive model achieve essentially identical accuracy
(R-squared of about `r round(reg$R2[1], 2)`), which indicates that the relationship between appliance usage
and consumption is close to linear. Bagged trees and random forests do not improve on the linear
model. The remaining unexplained variation is not captured by the available predictors.

```{r avp}
fig("13_actual_vs_predicted")
```

```{r gam}
fig("17_gam_smooth_effects")
```

```{r coef}
show(tab("linear_model_coefficients") |> dplyr::select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value, conf.low, conf.high))
```

Each additional air conditioner adds about 30 hours of monthly consumption, the largest per-unit effect.

# Peak Demand Classification

```{r cls}
show(cls)
```

```{r roc}
fig("18_roc_curves")
```

Logistic regression achieves the highest area under the ROC curve (`r round(cls$AUC[1], 3)`). With the default
0.5 threshold, recall is modest because peak households are a minority class. The threshold
analysis below shows the trade-off available to an operator who prefers to detect more peak households.

```{r thr}
fig("20_threshold_analysis")
```

```{r or}
fig("21_odds_ratios")
```

# Model Interpretation with LIME

```{r lime}
fig("22_lime_explanations")
```

LIME explanations show which appliance levels push an individual prediction towards or away from
peak demand. Permutation importance gives the global view.

```{r perm}
fig("23_permutation_importance")
```

Television, monitor, fan and air conditioner usage drive predictions; the city has no measurable
predictive contribution once appliance usage is known.

# Text Mining Supplement

The provider name is the only text field. Term frequencies of provider names are almost identical in
the peak and non-peak segments, so tf-idf scores are zero: provider vocabulary carries no
information about demand. This is reported as a negative result.

```{r terms}
fig("24_provider_terms")
```

# Conclusions

1. Consumption is driven by appliance usage and by the length of the month; city and provider add no
   predictive information.
2. Billing differences between cities reflect tariff rates, not behaviour.
3. A linear model explains roughly `r scales::percent(reg$R2[1], 1)` of the variance in monthly consumption, and
   logistic regression separates peak from non-peak households with an AUC of `r round(cls$AUC[1], 2)`.
4. High combined use of fans, televisions and monitors identifies the households most likely to be
   peak consumers.

# Limitations

* The data contain monthly totals, not interval readings; true time-of-day peaks cannot be studied.
* The appliance variables are usage levels whose exact units are not documented in the source file.
* The near-uniform distribution of cities, months and providers suggests the dataset may be synthetic or
  heavily standardised, which limits how far the findings generalise to real households.
* Roughly 43% of variance remains unexplained by the available features.
